## Analysis

The diff removes `case 'millisecond':` from the `parse` switch and adds `case "":`.

**The removal is observable.** The regex in `parse` is unchanged, so it still happily matches the unit `millisecond` (via `milliseconds?` with the optional `s`, case-insensitively). With `ms('1 millisecond')`, `match[2]` is `'millisecond'`, `type` becomes `'millisecond'`, which no longer matches any case label, so control falls to `default: return undefined;`. Before the change this returned `1`. So `ms('1 millisecond')` (and `'5 Millisecond'`, `'-1 millisecond'`, etc.) changes from a number to `undefined` — a caller-observable break.

**The addition is dead code.** `type` is computed as `(match[2] || 'ms').toLowerCase()`. Since `""` is falsy, an empty `match[2]` would become `'ms'` anyway; and the regex's unit group can only ever match a non-empty string (otherwise it simply doesn't participate and `match[2]` is `undefined`). So `type` can never be `""`, and even if it were, it would return `n`, identical to the `ms` case. The `case "":` addition changes nothing.

The library's own suite passes because it never exercises the singular full word `'millisecond'`, so the green suite masks the regression.

```json
{"defect": true, "testFile": {"path": "proof-test.js", "content": "var assert = require('assert');\nvar ms = require('./');\n\ndescribe('proof', function () {\n  it('parses the singular \"millisecond\" unit', function () {\n    assert.strictEqual(ms('1 millisecond'), 1);\n    assert.strictEqual(ms('5 Millisecond'), 5);\n    assert.strictEqual(ms('2 milliseconds'), 2);\n  });\n});\n"}, "note": "Removing `case 'millisecond':` makes the (unchanged) regex still match the unit but fall through to `default`, so ms('1 millisecond') returns undefined instead of 1. The added `case \"\":` is unreachable dead code because `(match[2] || 'ms')` never yields an empty string."}
```
